question.:question/worked-solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/generate/scratch/17592186110756-draft/plots/82121be02ef94e2343c1e00529c6c855cc8eadad2b04c4438b08cd8cc9f03c50.png)

Any point $(x,y)$ on the unit circle is related to the central angle $\theta$ as follows:

$$
x=cos⁡\theta ,\,y=sin⁡\theta
$$

We're given that $y=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, we have

$$
sin⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}.
$$

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $cos⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $sin⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{5}{9}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{4}{9}} \\  & =\pm \frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the positive answer since $cos⁡\theta$ is positive in the first quadrant. So, $cos⁡\theta =\frac{2}{3}.$

Knowing that $sec⁡\theta =\frac{1}{cos⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
sec⁡\theta =\frac{1}{(\frac{2}{3})}=\frac{3}{2}.
$$

The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that the $x$-coordinate of the point $P$ is $\frac{\sqrt{7}}{14},$ use the Pythagorean identity to find $csc⁡\theta .$
question.:question/worked-solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/generate/scratch/17592186110756-draft/plots/eecb61291888df883bc9658dfe60bf949e1897ee794daf86a40766ef84af820a.png)

Any point $(x,y)$ on the unit circle is related to the central angle $\theta$ as follows:

$$
x=cos⁡\theta ,\,y=sin⁡\theta
$$

We're given that $x=\frac{\sqrt{7}}{14}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, we have

$$
cos⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{7}}{14}.
$$

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $sin⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ sin⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $cos⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{7}}{14}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}sin⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{\sqrt{7}}{14})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{7}{196}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{189}{196}} \\  & =\pm \frac{3\sqrt{21}}{14}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the positive answer since $sin⁡\theta$ is positive in the first quadrant. So, $sin⁡\theta =\frac{3\sqrt{21}}{14}.$

Knowing that $csc⁡\theta =\frac{1}{sin⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}csc⁡\theta &=\frac{1}{(\frac{3\sqrt{21}}{14})}=\frac{14}{3\sqrt{21}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rationalize the denominator.

$$
\begin{aligned}csc⁡\theta  & =\frac{14}{3\sqrt{21}} \\  & =\frac{14}{3\sqrt{21}}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{21}}{\sqrt{21}} \\  & =\frac{14\sqrt{21}}{3\cdot 21} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{21}}{9}\end{aligned}
$$
